fragments.text: Distinguished colleagues, UNESCO partners, champions of universal information access. As we gather to celebrate the International Day for universal access to information, we face a key moment in this age, the digital age. Today marks the sixth AI for information access conference, building on years of crucial dialogue about how artificial intelligence can serve information accessibility, not as an abstract philosophical technological possibility, but as a fundamental human right that demands immediate coordinated action. Speaking from my experience working at the European Union level, I want to share how policy frameworks, public-private partnerships. Strategic regulation can transform artificial intelligence from a potential barrier into a powerful enabler of information accessibility for all. The European Union has positioned itself at the forefront of responsible AI governance, not merely from a regulatory point of view,

but as a moral imperative. The approach at the European Union recognizes that information accessibility is not just about technical capability, it's about ensuring that artificial intelligence systems serve human dignity and democratic values. Through the UAI Act, the EU established the world's first comprehensive AI regulation, creating binding obligations for high-risk AI systems that directly impact fundamental rights, including access to information. Regulation alone is insufficient, however. We need proactive policies that actively promote accessibility, not merely prevent harm. Consider the youth digital single market strategy, the youth accessibility art. These frameworks recognize that true digital inclusion requires intentional design, substantial investment, coordinated action, synergies across member states. these same principles must guide the approach to AI and information accessibility.

The challenge before us is not a technological challenge. It's fundamentally a political and economic one. AI systems capable of revolutionizing information access already exists. What's missing, however, is the policy architecture to ensure these capabilities is reach those who need them most. In my work, I've witnessed how policy can either accelerate or obstruct technological inclusion. When Estonia, pioneer digital governance making government services accessible online to all citizens, they didn't just adopt technology. They redesigned public service delivery around digital inclusion principles. When Finland guarantee broadband internet as a legal right. They recognize connectivity as essential infrastructure, not an add-on commercial luxury. These examples illuminate our path forward. AI for information accessibility requires

similar bold policy commitments, treating illiteracy as a public good, mandating accessibility features in AI systems accessing public information and creating public and infrastructure that serve citizens rather than shareholders. Working with private sector stakeholders across Europe, I've learned that the most successful AI accessibility initiatives emerge not from regulatory pressure alone, but recognizing the enormous market opportunity in inclusive design. When Microsoft invested heavily in AI-powered accessibility features, they didn't just serve users with disability, they created technologies that benefit everyone. Parents and multitask with audio content, professionals that work in noise environments, international audiences accessing content across language values. This is the power of universal design in AI. Solutions created for accessibility often deliver breakthrough

innovations for broader markets. The business case is before us. It's compelling. It requires however policy frameworks and architectures that reward long-term inclusive innovation over short-term profit maximization. One area where European experience offers particularly valuable lessons and we will discuss it right now is multilingual AI development. The EU commitment to linguistic diversity with 24 official languages and hundreds of regional languages has forced The European Union to confront AI's monolingual bias head on investments at your level in multilingual AI research through programs like Horizon Europe and the Digital Europe program demonstrate linguistic inclusions is not just possible technologically but it's essential and it's a fundamental part in AI legitimacy. When AI systems can operate effectively in Maltese, Irish

Gaelic and regional languages like Catalan or Welsh, they provide that the technological sophistication and cultural preservation can advance together. This European approach offers a model for global AI development rather than accepting English language as inevitable or dominant. We can invest in AI systems that truly serve global linguistic diversity. The window of shaping AI development around accessibility principles is rapidly closing. As AI systems become more entrenched, retrofitting accessibility becomes more difficult and expensive. I would say we have five years probably to embed accessibility into AI foundational architecture. After that, we'll spend decades, so much more time trying to fix systems designed without inclusion in mind. This is why events like today, AI for a conference are so crucial, and thank you for this opportunity.

They create the global dialogue necessary for coordinated action. Dialogue must lead to action, and action requires the political will to prioritise long-term accessibility, over-short-term convenience. In the European Union, we often speak of the Europe we want to build, vision of shared prosperity, fundamental rights, technological sovereignty aligned with democratic values. Today I invite you to think globally about the world we're choosing to build through our AI policies. We can build a world where a visually impaired student in rural Africa has the same access to educational content as a sighted student in downtown Brussels, mediated by AI systems that understand accessibility because it's built in, it's accessibility as a design principle and it's

not an afterthought. We can create a future where language barriers dissolve through AI translation that preserves cultural nuance and local knowledge, where information flows freely across borders while respecting privacy and security. But this future requires the same coordinated commitment that build the European project itself. The recognition that our individual prosperity depends on our collective commitment to both inclusion and justice. This is the choice, with faith. The choice is ours. The time is now. Let us choose wisely and let us choose together. Thank you very much.
